1.pericope_label: A mighty angel come down from heaven, clothed with a cloud, and a rainbow upon his head

schools.summary: Barnes places the vision between the sixth and seventh trumpets, argues from the order of events that the chapter concerns the Reformation, and draws no conclusion about the angel's identity beyond taking his strength to indicate great obstacles; Robertson denies twice that the cloud or the pillars prove the angel is Christ and calls him a special messenger of God distinct from the seven and the four.

Gill clears away the identifications offered by others, an emperor whose letters against the Arians were made the little book, the pope in either construction, and the reformers, and then refuses a created angel as well.

Clarke will go only as far as Christ or his representative, reading the cloud as a symbol of divine majesty and the feet of fire as rapidity and stability; Wesley denies the identification outright on the ground that the angel did not swear by himself, and defends each attribute as nothing too great for a creature.

Henry reads the description Christologically throughout: the cloud veils a glory too great for mortals and veils his dispensations, the rainbow shows him mindful of his covenant when his conduct is most mysterious, and the feet of fire that all his ways in grace and providence are pure and steady.

Victorinus identifies the angel with our Lord and reads the face of the resurrection and the rainbow of the judgment; Bede develops the same reading, making the cloud a cloud of flesh and the feet those that preach glad tidings, firm as pillars because James, Cephas and John seemed to be pillars of the Church.

positions.view: yes, the description belongs to no one else
Christ or his representative
no, a created angel, since he swears by another

outliers.claim: the chapter is coded history of the Protestant Reformation, following the fall of Constantinople treated in the previous chapter

themes: And I saw another mighty angel come down from heaven, clothed with a cloud: and a rainbow was upon his head, and his face was as it were the sun, and his feet as pillars of fire:

2.pericope_label: A little book open in his hand: he set his right foot upon the sea, and his left on the earth

schools.summary: Barnes treats the diminutive as deliberate, reasons from the emblem that an age characterised by a book must be meant, and applies it to the Reformation, tracing the movement to Wycliffe's suppressed New Testament and Luther's discovery of a Vulgate in the library at Erfurt; Robertson keeps the little roll distinct from the sealed scroll on grammatical grounds and locates its contents in the following chapter, and finds no significance in which foot rests where.
Gill argues the little book is the very scroll the Lamb unsealed and never laid down, so that the angel holding it must be the Lamb himself, and denies it is either the Bible or the gospel.

Clarke declines to identify it at all, saying it means some design of God long concealed and now to be made manifest, but who knows what it means, and takes the posture simply for universal command; Wesley makes the little book the remainder of the other, notes that from this point the vision speaks more clearly, and works out the angel's orientation in detail.

positions.view: the same scroll opened by the Lamb in the earlier vision
the remainder of that scroll, now given opened to John
a different and smaller book, deliberately distinguished
unknowable

debates.question: Does the placing of the feet signify anything?

positions.view: no; it is a bold and graphic picture with no special point
yes; the orientation, the beasts of sea and land, and possibly Europe and Asia

outliers.claim: if one were asked to devise an emblem of the Reformation, nothing better could be chosen than an angel holding a book out to mankind

themes: And he had in his hand a little book open: and he set his right foot upon the sea, and his left foot on the earth,

3.pericope_label: Seven thunders uttered their voices: seal them up, and write them not

schools.summary: Barnes refuses to specify what the angel cried, canvasses the editors over the definite article and concludes the number is specific, then applies the thunders to the papal anathemas issuing from the seven-hilled city against the Reformers; Ellicott insists on the seven thunders as a fourth Apocalyptic order of sevens beside the seals, trumpets and vials, rejects the guesses that they are the trumpets or the crusades, and reads the prohibition as meaning the utterances were for those who heard them; Robertson calls the group recognised but unexplained and thinks it idle to conjecture their content.
Gill supposes the cry was the book of prophecy concerning the church.

Wesley makes the speakers glorious heavenly powers, and observes that this is the only thing in the vision John is told to keep secret, so that something peculiarly secret was revealed to him beyond all that is written.
Henry states plainly that we know neither the subjects of the thunders nor the reason for suppressing them, and that there are great events in history which open prophecy does not notice.
Bede identifies the seven thunders with the seven trumpets and reads the roar as the Church filled with sevenfold grace lifting up her voice to preach.

positions.view: the same as the seven trumpets
the papal bulls of excommunication thundered from the seven hills of Rome
a fourth order of sevens whose content is never revealed, perhaps further judgments
unknowable; it is idle to conjecture

outliers.claim: the crowd heard thunder and some thought an angel spoke, while Christ heard articulate words, so dull ears hear thunder and never the voice of God

themes: And cried with a loud voice, as when a lion roareth: and when he had cried, seven thunders uttered their voices.
And when the seven thunders had uttered their voices, I was about to write: and I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Seal up those things which the seven thunders uttered, and write them not.

5.pericope_label: He sware by him that liveth for ever, that there should be time no longer

schools.summary: Barnes and Robertson identify the raised hand as the customary oath posture, and Robertson argues that swearing by another proves this angel is not Christ and that the clause denies further delay rather than the existence of time; Barnes reads the oath as a rebuke to the Reformers' widespread expectation of an imminent end, documenting it from a note in Melancthon's hand in Luther's Bible and from Latimer's arithmetic and preaching.

Gill explains the formula of swearing by the living God as distinguishing him from idols without breath and asserting that he has life in himself, independently, as the fountain of life to every creature.

Wesley notes that only the seventh trumpet is confirmed by an oath, reads the angel's posture as comprehending heaven, sea and land against every quarter where enemies remain, and takes the denied time as a technical period of some eleven centuries, dating the interval from the year 800 to 1836.
Henry sets the two readings side by side without choosing, either no further delay once the last angel sounds, or time itself swallowed up in eternity when the mystery is finished.

debates.question: What does it mean that there should be time no longer?

positions.view: no further delay in fulfilling the seventh trumpet
time itself ceasing, swallowed up in eternity
a technical period is denied, allowing a datable interval to be computed

outliers.claim: the interval runs from the year 800, when Charles the Great instituted a new line of emperors, to the year 1836

themes: And the angel which I saw stand upon the sea and upon the earth lifted up his hand to heaven,

And sware by him that liveth for ever and ever, who created heaven, and the things that therein are, and the earth, and the things that therein are, and the sea, and the things which are therein, that there should be time no longer:

7.pericope_label: The mystery of God shall be finished: take it, and eat it up

schools.summary: Barnes takes the mystery for the divine purpose concealed and progressively unfolded through the prophets, makes the seventh trumpet the close of this series of visions with a new series beginning afterwards, insists the eating is symbolic throughout, and finds in the angel's readiness to surrender the book an image of God putting his Bible into men's hands against every effort to restrain its circulation; Robertson glosses the mystery as the whole purpose of God in human history.

Gill fills the mystery with the thousand years of Christ's kingdom on earth, a time of unspeakable light after the darkness of early heresies, of the barbarian invasions, and of the smoke of the pit, and asks where one should go for knowledge but to him who has the words of eternal life.

Clarke refuses to say what the mystery is, notes the little agreement among learned men, and rebukes the confidence with which they speak of hidden things, offering only that the trumpet probably belongs to the Jewish state; Wesley distinguishes the word of God fulfilled by the destruction of the beast from the mystery fulfilled by the removal of the dragon.

Henry draws the lesson from the order of the commands, that the messenger must digest what he has discovered before publishing it, explains the sweetness and the bitterness from the pleasure of foreseeing and the pain of what was foreseen, and concludes that God's servants must deliver every message whether it pleases men or not.

debates.question: What is the mystery that shall be finished?

positions.view: the divine purpose concealed and unfolded through the prophets
the thousand years of Christ’s kingdom on earth
the removal of the dragon, distinct from the destruction of the beast
unknown; the learned do not agree

outliers.claim: and yet with what confidence do men speak of the meaning of these hidden things

themes: But in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he shall begin to sound, the mystery of God should be finished, as he hath declared to his servants the prophets.
And the voice which I heard from heaven spake unto me again, and said, Go and take the little book which is open in the hand of the angel which standeth upon the sea and upon the earth.
And I went unto the angel, and said unto him, Give me the little book. And he said unto me, Take it, and eat it up; and it shall make thy belly bitter, but it shall be in thy mouth sweet as honey.

10.pericope_label: Sweet as honey in my mouth, and bitter in my belly: thou must prophesy again

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the sweetness beside Ezekiel and the psalmist and makes it a condition of ministry that the man who will endure bitterness must first have tasted the sweetness, supplies the bitterness from what fidelity cost the older prophets, and ties the renewed commission to the vision of the two witnesses who prophesy mightily and in vain; Ellicott and Robertson both read the verb as an indefinite plural and the preposition as concerning rather than before, and Robertson notes the order of results is given as actually experienced.

Clarke finds in the roll some pleasing and some unpleasing intelligence, then closes the chapter by declaring that he does not understand these prophecies and will not explain them, rebuking the learned who trifle in solemn things, and rejecting by name the computation of an artificial period of eleven hundred and eleven years; Wesley reads the charge as fulfilled by the measuring of the temple and lists the succeeding kingdoms.

debates.question: Should the chapter’s prophetic scheme be construed at all?

positions.view: no; the prophecies are not understood, and the chronological computation is inadmissible
yes; the interval and the succeeding kingdoms can be identified

outliers.claim: rejects by name the chronos scheme of eleven hundred and eleven years with its half-period and non-period, the very reading Wesley adopts earlier in the chapter

themes: And I took the little book out of the angel’s hand, and ate it up; and it was in my mouth sweet as honey: and as soon as I had eaten it, my belly was bitter.
And he said unto me, Thou must prophesy again before many peoples, and nations, and tongues, and kings.
